rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The intermediate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Change temperature alone to test selectivity in the crowded central cluster and late doublet. The short elution window leaves ample room for a shallower gradient if temperature does not resolve these pairs.

Test the low-temperature endpoint with the same gradient to map the strong temperature-dependent selectivity. This may spread the central cluster and avoid the near-coelution seen at 60 C before we optimize gradient slope.
Keep the best temperature and make the gradient shallower to improve the two unresolved pairs. The current last peak at 7.30 min provides room to gain resolution before incurring a time penalty.

Use a shallower gradient to further separate the remaining critical pair, while raising the starting organic fraction to offset the added retention time. The first peak was well isolated, leaving room to increase the starting strength.
Reduce the gradient slope further to target the sole remaining unresolved pair, currently at R = 1.09. Raising the starting organic fraction modestly should help keep the last peak below 10 min.
The maximum CRF is achieved; now shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. This tests whether the critical pair's R = 1.61 margin can tolerate the steeper slope.

Raise the starting organic fraction to shorten retention while restoring a slightly shallower slope than the fully resolved injection 6. This tests whether the critical pair remains resolved with a narrower gradient window; injection 6 remains the benchmark.

Keep the same gradient slope as injection 8 but shift the starting composition higher to test for renewed separation beyond the near-coelution. This could yield a substantially faster fully resolved method, while injection 6 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Shift the starting composition up another step while maintaining the successful gradient slope. All pairs currently have resolution margin, so this tests whether retention can be shortened further without losing full resolution.

Return to the starting composition of the fastest fully resolved method and shorten its gradient by one step. This tests a smaller speed increase without the resolution loss caused by starting at 0.40 organic.

Shorten the gradient another step while retaining the successful starting composition and temperature. The minimum resolution of 1.93 leaves margin to reduce elution time while preserving the maximum CRF.
Continue shortening the gradient by one grid step, since every pair remains comfortably resolved. Monitor the late doublet and the central pair whose resolution decreased as the gradient steepened.
Shorten the gradient one more step to reduce analysis time while retaining the maximum score. The late doublet is now limiting at R = 2.01, still above the full-resolution threshold.
Reduce gradient duration by another grid step while holding composition and temperature fixed. The late doublet retains enough resolution margin to test a faster separation.
Shorten the gradient one step further to seek a faster maximum-score method. Monitor both the late doublet and the central pair at R = 1.96, as both lose resolution with increasing slope.

Test the next shorter gradient to establish the full-resolution boundary. The two limiting pairs are close to R = 1.5, so injection 16 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback if this step is too steep.

Restore the shortest fully resolved gradient and raise temperature by one step to test a different route to faster elution. This isolates the temperature effect on the two limiting pairs while retaining injection 16 as the benchmark.

Test a faster, higher-temperature region where the central pair may separate again after an elution-order reversal. This is an exploratory selectivity test; injection 16 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Make the latest gradient shallower to test whether its moderately unresolved pairs can reach R ≥ 1.5 while retaining a short elution window. Injection 16 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Narrow the gradient window while preserving injection 16's successful slope of 0.05 organic fraction per minute. The gradient ends at the outlet at 4.65 min, after its last peak at 4.14 min, so this should retain full resolution with a much shorter programmed gradient.

Test a gradient slope of 0.055 per minute, between the fully resolved 0.050 and the insufficiently resolved 0.060. This refines the speed–resolution boundary while keeping injection 21 as the compact maximum-score fallback.

Test whether a further increase in starting organic restores central-pair separation beyond the loss seen at 0.40, keeping the same slope as injections 9 and 10. This explores a potentially faster fully resolved region while retaining injection 21 as the confirmed maximum-score fallback.

Test the minimum programmed gradient duration while preserving the successful initial slope of injection 21. The central cluster should elute before the gradient ends at the outlet; the subsequent hold tests whether the late peaks remain fully resolved and elute within 10 minutes.

Use the final injection to test a compact method with a shallower gradient for greater resolution margin and a stronger final hold than injection 24 to limit late-peak retention. Injection 21 remains the fastest confirmed compact method achieving the maximum CRF.
